<reason>Both sides were competent and disciplined. PRO's best weapon was the inattention dilemma ("if labels are useless, your unit-price enforcement dies too"), but CON escaped it credibly in B4.1: attention is scarce, not zero, and the unit price is the one number that earns the single glance at the shelf, while the flag adds a competing second read. CON then landed the debate's most damaging sequence: PRO's own A2 answer conceded the flag's decisive effect is that the shopper "switches, buys the competitor," which CON reframed as steering to worse purchases when the shrunk brand is still cheaper per gram — a point PRO's closing answered only by re-asserting that switching is the sanction working. CON also tracked the compliance creep from "a line of code" to "substantially similar" adjudication, and the observation that a 12-month window lets 3% annual shrinks slip through entirely went unanswered. PRO's "evasion is no reason to legalize concealment" and the visibility-norm argument were solid, but CON's neutrality response (both price rises and size trims are legitimate, both already disclosed) blunted them. CON made the debate easier to decide with the memorable "information that improves the purchase versus information that provokes a reaction" frame, and answered pressure questions more cleanly. Slight execution costs on both sides from clipped turns, slightly heavier for A (opening clipped mid-paternalism answer).</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5: CON seized on PRO's admission that the flag's changed decision is "switches, buys the competitor" and showed the unit price already settles whether the competitor is better value today — turning PRO's resentment-as-sanction framing into "distortion by resentment." PRO never fully recovered, and B4.1's "attention is scarce, not zero" simultaneously defused PRO's sharpest dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
